insight.title: The Moon Was Once A Close Neighbor
insight.subtitle: When the Moon first formed, it orbited just 14,000 miles from Earth’s surface.
insight.notificationHook: The Moon used to be much closer

sections.text: Four billion years ago, the Moon did not appear as a small, distant disk in the night sky. It loomed as a massive, glowing sphere, appearing fifteen times larger than it does today.

Tidal forces were so violent that the Earth experienced massive, daily swells. The proximity of the Moon pulled at the liquid crust, creating an alien landscape of constant, shifting motion under a molten sky.
As the Moon slowly spiraled outward to its current distance, the Earth’s rotation began to decelerate. Our planet’s long, calm days are a direct consequence of that ancient, celestial retreat.
We live in the wake of a retreating giant.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow will no longer consider a moratorium on strikes in the Black Sea or on energy infrastructure. Putin vowed a harsh response after Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week. He spoke after holding three-way talks with the Chinese and US presidents at an APEC summit in Shenzhen. Putin said the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not for military equipment. He stated that the road section suffered serious damage and would be restored.

Bank of Japan governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank will keep raising interest rates. Ueda projected that consumer spending will recover from a soft patch following a drop in third-quarter GDP data. He signaled that the central bank is vigilant about the inflationary impact of the weak yen. The yen has dropped 1.8 percent for the year to date to trade near 160 per dollar. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the central bank to raise interest rates in December.

International health authorities formally announced that the United States has lost its measles elimination status. The designation was won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. Public health experts and political leaders called the backslide a national embarrassment. The US has recorded over 5,400 measles cases this year, which is more than any other year since 1991. An explosive outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases, while 10 deaths have been confirmed across three states.

The United States Commerce Department issued an interim final rule barring foreign data centers with American AI chips from providing cloud service to businesses in two dozen countries. Those countries include China, Iran and Russia. The new rule also restricts American companies from shipping high-end AI chips to five countries without government approval. Those countries include Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. China censured the move, calling it an abuse of export control measures.

Rapid immigration helped turn Spain into one of Europe's biggest economic success stories. Opinion polls put the conservative People's Party ahead before Spain's November 29 election, but show it would likely need an alliance with the far-right Vox to govern. Vox advocates sharp cuts to immigration, ending regularization of new arrivals, and increasing deportations. Foreign-born workers account for 14 percent of Spain's population and over 16 percent of the workforce. Immigrants accounted for around half of Spain's GDP growth between 2022 and 2025.

Amazon and Google own 28 percent of Anthropic as the AI startup starts trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Amazon holds 14.6 percent and Google holds 13.4 percent of Class N stock, which has no vote. Google’s stake includes about $10 billion of a $26 billion private placement at the $83 IPO price. Anthropic has committed to spend at least about $121.3 billion with Google between April 2026 and July 2033, and at least $110 billion with Amazon between May 2026 and April 2036.

Turning to technology, a US official rushed Nvidia H200 approvals for China, according to a report from The Information.

A senior United States export official has pushed staff to fast-track Nvidia H200 chip sales to China. Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Bureau of Industry and Security, has applied the pressure in recent months. In some cases, Kessler told staff to approve exports over objections from other government departments. The H200 came out in twenty twenty-three and is a generation behind Nvidia Blackwell chips. President Donald Trump approved it for sale to China in December twenty twenty-five. Nvidia agreed to give the United States government a twenty-five percent cut of its H200 sales to China. Nvidia has stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China, and the H200 belongs to that family. Huang is due before three House committees on December first.

Next, Meta greenhouse gas emissions increased significantly due to its growing artificial intelligence infrastructure. Meta emissions surged forty-five percent last year amid an artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. That surge prompted the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by twenty thirty.

Turning to technology, the United Kingdom government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide encrypted customer information. The ruling came from the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders. The tribunal rejected the Home Office claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security. The order was a technical capabilities notice, and Apple refused to comply. Apple blocked United Kingdom users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud. The secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals data stored in encrypted cloud storage. Rights group Liberty International brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals. A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

In business news, India is imposing an effective duty of one hundred sixty-two point five percent on bulk Scotch imports amid a dispute over a trade agreement. The India-United Kingdom trade agreement, implemented in July, halved tariffs on Scotch to seventy-five percent. Indian investigators argue that companies are using incorrect customs classifications for bulk Scotch concentrates. Since May, the imports have been classified under a customs category for compound alcoholic preparations, which attracts a one hundred fifty percent tariff. A consumption tax takes the total duty to one hundred sixty-two point five percent. Thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than eighty shipping containers remain stuck at ports. Seventy percent of the goods value must be paid upfront under a provisional release arrangement. Shares of Diageo in France and Pernod in London fell by one point five percent and one point twenty-five percent following the report. About eighty percent of Scotch whisky imports from Britain arrive in bulk.

In health news, the United States government is relocating its remaining laboratory chimpanzees to a permanent sanctuary. The last chimpanzees owned by the United States government and still living in a laboratory will be moved to a sanctuary next year.

Finally, Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide and provide support for people who have tried to take their own lives. Attempted suicide remains punishable under provisions of Nigeria criminal and penal codes. Convicted individuals face a fine, up to a year in jail, or both. The legislation would require authorities to provide rehabilitation services and promote wider access to mental healthcare. If passed, the measure would align Nigeria with a growing number of countries that have removed criminal penalties for attempted suicide.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Four billion years ago, the Moon did not appear as a small, distant disk in the night sky. It orbited just fourteen thousand miles from Earth surface. It loomed as a massive, glowing sphere, appearing fifteen times larger than it does today. Tidal forces were so violent that the Earth experienced massive, daily swells. The proximity of the Moon pulled at the liquid crust, creating an alien landscape of constant motion under a molten sky. As the Moon slowly spiraled outward to its current distance, the Earth rotation began to decelerate. Our planet long, calm days are a direct consequence of that ancient retreat. We live in the wake of a retreating giant. What might the night sky look like billions of years from now?

Thank you for listening to this edition of the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is the full analysis, not the quick version. 

Will Russia agree to a truce in the Black Sea or on energy sites? Russian President Vladimir Putin said no to any truce after Ukraine hit the bridge linking Russia to Crimea. 

For years, Russia and Ukraine have been locked in a bitter war. Russia illegally annexed the Crimean Peninsula in twenty fourteen. Since then, Moscow has used Crimea as a massive military base. Russia uses it to launch air strikes and to supply its troops in southern Ukraine. Because the bridge is so important for moving weapons and supplies, Ukraine has tried to hit it many times. It was built in twenty eighteen, and it is a twelve-mile bridge. 

The situation turned into news because Ukraine struck the bridge for the third time in a week. This attack used Neptune cruise missiles. It destroyed the central road section of the bridge. Part of it collapsed into the water. 

Today, Vladimir Putin said Moscow will no longer consider a moratorium on strikes in the Black Sea or on energy infrastructure. He spoke at a press conference in Shenzhen. He had just held talks with the Chinese and United States presidents. Putin claimed the bridge was used only for civilian purposes. But he vowed that Russia's response will be far more painful than what Ukraine did to the bridge. Russia's transport ministry said nobody was hurt. Train services have resumed, but car traffic is banned for the foreseeable future because a section about two hundred meters or six hundred sixty feet long was dragged into the sea. 

This is happening now because the latest strike caused the worst damage to the structure in several years. Putin also just held high-profile talks with world leaders. 

For the listener, this means the war could get much worse. The road repair could take a long time and happen under Ukrainian fire. Watch for how Russia chooses to strike back. 

Now let us turn to Japan and its interest rates. 

Will Japan keep raising interest rates even if consumer spending looks soft? Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said yes, the central bank will keep raising rates. 

Japan's central bank spent fourteen years trying to hit its price target. It finally achieved this goal recently. To keep the economy stable, the bank wants to raise interest rates step by step. But the weak yen has been a big problem. The yen is the currency used in Japan. A weak yen makes the cost of imported raw materials go up. That pushes up prices for food and daily necessities. It has dropped nearly two percent for the year to trade near one hundred sixty per dollar. 

The news changed when third-quarter gross domestic product data showed a drop in private consumption. Some analysts worried this drop would slow down future rate hikes. 

Today, Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda brushed off those worries. He said consumer spending is still resilient as a whole. He explained that the drop came from the rising cost of living and bad weather. Ueda signaled a near-term rate hike, possibly as soon as December. He noted that firms are now more active in passing rising costs on to shoppers. The central bank raised its policy rate to one point two five percent in September. Most analysts expect another hike by the end of March. 

This is happening now because stubbornly high energy costs and import prices keep adding to inflation. 

For the listener, this means borrowing costs in Japan could go up very soon. Watch for the December central bank meeting and whether the yen gets even weaker. 

Now let us look at the news about measles in the United States. 

How did the United States lose its measles elimination status? International health authorities announced that the US lost this status because a single measles virus spread continuously for twelve months. 

Measles is a very contagious virus. In the year two thousand, the United States won elimination status after decades of vaccination efforts. This meant the disease was no longer constantly spreading inside the country. But over time, vaccination rates dropped in some places. People traveled back and forth across borders, carrying the virus with them. 

The situation turned into news when international health authorities officially stripped the US of its elimination status. 

Today, public health experts call this a shameful national embarrassment. The decision was based on data from January twenty twenty-five to January twenty twenty-six. Officials confirmed that a single viral lineage started on January twentieth, twenty twenty-five, in Texas. That single outbreak led to a twelve-month chain of cases. The Pan American Health Organization said a massive outbreak in Pennsylvania with over fifteen hundred cases did not even factor into the decision because it started later, in April. This year, the US has already seen over five, four hundred cases, which is more than any year since nineteen ninety-one. There have been ten confirmed deaths across three states. 

This is happening now because health committees reviewed the genetic and epidemiological data collected over the past year. 

For the listener, this means a preventable disease is spreading again because of a lack of vaccination. Watch for whether the government releases the full private data and if case numbers keep rising. 

Now let us turn to how United States controls flow of advanced tech, chip, and compute to China.

How does the U.S. government stop advanced technology from reaching rival nations? It uses trade rules and export bans to control where high-end computer chips can go. 

Let us go back to how this started. Over a decade ago, lawmakers in Washington began talking about keeping advanced technology out of China. They wanted a legal tool to control how technology moves around the world. That legal weapon took shape during the first term of Donald Trump. His administration passed the Export Control Reform Act in twenty eighteen. This law let the U.S. government control advanced technology that started inside the country. The main goal was to stop top-tier computer chips from going to countries like China, Russia, and Iran. These chips have a dual use. That means they can be used for normal business or for military work. 

The situation turned into news because of a new rule. On November sixteenth, twenty twenty-six, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim final rule. This is a temporary rule that takes effect right away. It stops data center operators outside the U.S. from giving cloud computing services to businesses in two dozen countries. Those countries include China, Iran, and Russia. 

Today's news brings even tighter limits. The new rule also stops American companies from freely shipping high-end artificial intelligence chips to five countries. Those countries are Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and two others. Companies need explicit approval from the U.S. government to make those shipments. China has censured the move. It called the action another case of the U.S. overstretching national security and abusing export controls to interfere in normal trade. 

This is happening right now because of a high-level meeting. The new rule came just days before U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping were set to meet in Shenzhen, China. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the APEC Summit on November eighteenth and nineteenth. 

For the listener, this means global tech supply chains face more friction. Trade rules could get stricter. As for what to watch next, it is possible that China will announce counter-measures or new trade restrictions of its own. 

Now let us turn to Spain, where a fast-growing population of migrants helped fuel an economic boom. Could a new right-wing government slow that growth down? 

Let us look at how Spain got here. In recent years, rapid immigration helped turn Spain into one of Europe's biggest economic success stories. When Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez came to power in twenty eighteen, he made a pro-immigration strategy a pillar of his economic plan. His Socialist party expanded recruitment of workers in their home countries, sped up the recognition of foreign degrees, and made it easier for migrants to get jobs. Since twenty twenty-two, the number of foreign workers in Spain has grown by more than 1.2 million. Today, foreign-born people make up fourteen percent of Spain's population of nearly fifty million. Immigrants make up over sixteen percent of the workforce. Roughly half of these overseas workers come from Latin America, according to the national statistics institute. According to the Bank of Spain, immigrants accounted for about half of Spain's economic growth between twenty twenty-two and twenty-five. That equals 1.7 percentage points of growth. They also drove more than two-thirds of all new jobs in that same period. 

The situation changed because of upcoming elections. Opinion polls put the conservative People's Party ahead of the ruling Socialists before Spain's November twenty-ninth election. But the polls show the conservatives would likely need an alliance with the far-right, anti-immigrant party called Vox to form a government. 

Today's news is that investors are worried about what an anti-immigration government might do to the economy. The People's Party wants to end what its leader calls uncontrolled immigration while still allowing some workers in to cover labor shortages. Vox goes much further. Vox wants sharp cuts to immigration, more deportations, and priority for Spanish citizens in public services. Economics professors and analysts warn that these tighter rules could weigh on labor force growth and erode Spain's economic advantage over the rest of Europe. Spain's economy grew by 2.6 percent last year, which is double the euro zone average. The government expects growth to stay at 2.6 percent this year and 2.2 percent in twenty twenty-seven. 

This is happening now because the election is at the end of November. Voters are heading to the polls while the country deals with other pressures, including a housing crisis and a general strike called this month. 

For the listener, this shows how closely economic growth can tie to population changes. As for what to watch next, it is possible that a new coalition government will pass strict new limits on arrivals, which could slow down job market growth. 

Next, let us look at Amazon and Google, which spent years building artificial intelligence models to compete with Anthropic. How do they also end up owning nearly thirty percent of it? 

Let us trace how this partnership grew. Anthropic is an artificial intelligence startup that makes a popular model called Claude. Over the last three years, Big Tech companies poured billions of dollars into Anthropic to help it build and train its technology. Google invested more than twelve billion dollars since twenty twenty-three. Amazon put about eighteen billion dollars into the company. At the same time, Anthropic agreed to buy massive amounts of cloud computing power and chips from both tech giants. They became investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors all at once. Regulators in Washington, including the Federal Trade Commission, looked into these deals over concerns about deep conflicts of interest. 

The situation changed when Anthropic went public. Anthropic held its initial public offering on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT. 

Today's news is the result of that public debut. Anthropic priced its shares at eighty-three dollars each. At that price, Amazon holds a 14.6 percent stake in Anthropic, and Google holds 13.4 percent. All of their shares are non-voting stock, which means they do not get a say in how the company is run. Anthropic's seven co-founders keep control through a single share held in a special company. Alongside the IPO, Google and other hardware giants like Nvidia and Microsoft joined a twenty-six billion dollar private placement at the IPO price. Amazon and Google are now sitting on a combined paper gain of roughly two hundred sixty billion dollars, according to financial reports. 

This is happening now because market conditions allowed Anthropic to make its giant public debut and turn private investments into liquid public stock. 

For the listener, this massive valuation highlights how much money is flowing through the artificial intelligence boom. Watch next to see if public market investors keep funding these high server costs, or if the growth slows down. 

Now let us turn to US officials who rushed Nvidia H200 approvals for China, according to a report by The Information.

Why did a top official push to get certain computer chips into China? A government leader pressured staff to approve sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to Chinese buyers.

Nvidia is a big American company that makes powerful computer chips. These chips are essential for building advanced artificial intelligence. The United States government has rules that limit selling these high-tech tools to China. These rules exist because officials worry that China could use the technology for military projects.

The H200 chip is a newer version of older technology. It came out in twenty twenty-three. It is not as fast as Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell chips. In December twenty twenty-five, President Donald Trump allowed the H200 to be sold to China. This happened after Jensen Huang, the head of Nvidia, spent a lot of time lobbying the government. In exchange for this approval, Nvidia agreed to give the U.S. government a twenty-five percent cut of the money made from these sales.

Even with that deal, the chips have not been moving quickly. Reports show that many H200 chips are sitting in storage in Hong Kong. This is because officials in Beijing have been slow to give their own approvals. On a recent call with investors, Nvidia’s leader Colette Kress said the company has stopped selling these specific chips to China for now.

Now, reports say Jeffrey Kessler, a senior official in charge of export rules, has been pushing his staff to speed up these sales. He reportedly told his team to approve the exports even when other government departments disagreed. This is happening as Washington is taking a closer look at Nvidia’s business in China. Congress is currently working on stricter rules for chip sales. Jensen Huang is expected to answer questions from three House committees on December first.

This situation matters because it shows a conflict between business goals and national security. It is possible that Congress will pass new laws to make these sales harder. We will have to watch if the government changes its approach to these chip exports after the upcoming hearings.

Next, we look at how a major tech company is changing its plans because of the environment.

Meta is rethinking its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by twenty thirty. The company’s greenhouse gas emissions grew by forty-five percent last year. This increase happened because Meta is building more infrastructure to support its artificial intelligence projects. This trend is also appearing at other large tech firms as they race to build more data centers.

Now, let us turn to a legal battle in Britain about secret government demands.

Why was the British government forced to admit it sent a secret order to Apple? A court ruled that the government must confirm it demanded a way to bypass Apple’s security to see private data.

Apple makes iPhones and provides a service called iCloud. This service stores photos and files for millions of people. In twenty twenty-two, Apple launched a feature called Advanced Data Protection. This feature uses end-to-end encryption. That means only the user can see their own data, and even Apple cannot unlock it.

In twenty twenty-five, the British government issued a secret order to Apple. It was a technical capability notice. This is an official demand for a company to change how its products work. The government wanted Apple to create a backdoor. That is a secret way for authorities to get inside the system and see customer information. The law at the time said Apple could not even tell anyone it had received this order.

Apple refused to build the backdoor. Instead, the company stopped offering its Advanced Data Protection feature to new users in the United Kingdom. Apple did this because the company says it has never built a master key for its products and never will. Even though the details leaked to the press, Apple was still legally blocked from talking about the order.

The group Liberty International took the case to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal. This is a special British court that hears complaints about government spying. The court ruled that the government failed to prove that keeping the order secret was necessary for national security. This means Apple can now speak openly about the demand.

This is happening because the legal battle has moved into the light. It is the first time the government has been forced to confirm such a secret order exists. The court’s decision is a win for those who want more transparency in how governments use their power. While the actual requirement for a backdoor still exists, Apple can now challenge that demand in an open court. We expect a final hearing on what specific details can be shared to happen sometime next year.

Next, India imposes a one hundred sixty-two point five percent duty and tax on bulk Scotch imports amid a United Kingdom trade pact dispute.

Why is a bottle of Scotch whisky costing so much more in India right now?
India is charging a big new tax on bulk Scotch imports because of a trade fight with Britain.
For many years, the Indian government has charged heavy taxes on foreign drinks.
This is to protect local makers of alcohol.
People around the world love Scotch whisky.
India is the biggest market for Scotch by volume.
Britain and India worked for years on a trade deal to lower these taxes.
The deal started in July.
It cut taxes on Scotch in half, down to seventy-five percent.
Big drink companies like Pernod Ricard and Diageo were very happy.
They bring in Scotch in large containers, which is called bulk Scotch.
Then they mix it with other spirits to make cheaper drinks for the huge Indian market.
About eighty percent of Scotch imports from Britain arrive in this way.
Then something changed.
Indian investigators looked closely at how companies bring in this bulk Scotch.
They decided the companies used the wrong customs category.
The investigators put bulk Scotch into a new category for raw materials used to make drinks.
This new category has a tax of one hundred fifty percent.
Then the government added a local consumption tax on top of that.
Now the total tax and duty add up to one hundred sixty-two point five percent.
This is even higher than the old tax of one hundred fifty percent before the trade deal.
Today, thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than eighty shipping containers are stuck at ports.
The containers belong to big makers like Pernod, Diageo, and Bacardi.
To get their drinks out, companies must pay seventy-five percent of the value upfront.
They also have to use bank guarantees for the rest of the money.
Smaller Indian companies that also import Scotch could face big problems.
They might struggle to find the money for these bank guarantees.
The British government says it is working with New Delhi to fix the issue.
India says the dispute will be settled soon.
This is happening now because investigators want to stop what they call misclassification.
They say it causes a big loss of money for the government.
Pernod and Diageo shares fell in Europe after the news came out.
